title: Ziggurat of Ur
summary: The Ziggurat of Ur is the stepped mud-brick temple platform raised for the moon god Nanna at Ur in southern Mesopotamia, begun by King Ur-Nammu around 2100 BCE. The Neo-Babylonian king Nabonidus rebuilt its upper stages in the 6th century BCE, and the lower stage was restored in the 1980s.

uncertainty.note: Start is 'around 2100 B.C.E.' (Khan Academy), astronomical -2099. A 1924 Penn Museum report, using the chronology of its day, dated Ur-Engur (Ur-Nammu) and Dungi to about 2300 BC. End is the present: the lower stage still stands.

phases.description: Begun by Ur-Nammu around 2100 BCE; per the 1924 Penn report he and his son Dungi left the tower unfinished.
Lowest stage of Ur-Nammu stands (the upper stages are not known).
Nabonidus, last king of Babylon, replaced the upper terraces in the 6th century BCE, building over the Ur-Nammu stage.
The 1924 Penn report places the ziggurat's destruction in the fifth century BC; the lower stage survived as a mound until excavation.
In the 1980s the facade of the lower foundation and its three staircases were restored.

materials.material: mud-brick core covered with baked bricks laid in bitumen

reviewer_note: Shape ziggurat. Least sure of the height: the only figure from a museum page is Penn Museum's 92 feet (28 m) from a 1924 restoration plan, while Khan Academy gives 21 to 30 m; the 1924 lower stage (130 x 195 ft) also disagrees with the 64 x 46 m base used here, which is the modern summary figure. Khan Academy renders its text by script, so the spotcheck tool cannot fetch it; its figures were read through a text proxy. The 'ruined' start (fifth century BC) follows the 1924 report. Coordinates: OSM way and UNESCO Ur component agree to about 30 m.
